Malaria remains one of the most significant public health challenges in many low- and middle-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. To make surveillance a more effective and efficient core intervention, there is a need to shift from reactive to predictive approaches by using models to forecast malaria risk. Our work on malaria early warning systems has involved developing and testing predictive models for malaria forecasting and outbreak detection in the epidemic-prone Amhara region of Ethiopia ([Midekisa et al. 2012](#malaria-refs), [Davis et al. 2019](#malaria-refs), [Nekorchuk et al. 2021](#malaria-refs)). These studies have emphasized the importance of accounting for spatial heterogeneity in the lagged effects of climate drivers. We have also evaluated the accuracy of different sources of geospatial environmental data ([Alemu and Wimberly 2020](#malaria-refs)) and developed informatics tools to facilitate access to satellite Earth observations for malaria early warning ([Liu et al. 2015](#malaria-refs), [Wimberly et al. 2022](#malaria-refs)).

Working with partners in the Ethiopian public health sector, we co-developed the Epidemic Prognosis Incorporating Disease and Environmental Modeling for Integrated Assessment (EPIDEMIA) system for implementing malaria forecasting ([Merkord et al. 2017](#malaria-refs)). We conducted a pilot study implementing EPIDEMIA in the Ahmara region and conducted a scoping study to develop a roadmap for scaling malaria early warning to a national level ([Wimberly and Nekorchuk 2021](#malaria-refs)). EPIDEMIA is programmed using the R language adn environment for statistical computing, and the code is freely available on GitHub. Visit the [EPIDEMIA](http://ecograph.net/epidemia/) page for more links to the software and documentation. We are currently developing [EPIDEMIA 2.0](http://ecograph.net/epidemia/), a next-generation version of EPIDEMIA with an improved user interface and enhanced capabilities for malaria modeling and prediction.
